# Problem

Derive the form of

$$
p(y_0\mid \mathbf y,X,\mathbf x_0)
$$

in equation (6.19), using the usual conditional-normal formulae.

# Conditional distribution of a partitioned normal vector

Given the joint normal distribution

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf Y_1\\
\mathbf Y_2
\end{pmatrix}
\sim
N\left[
\begin{pmatrix}
\boldsymbol\mu_1\\
\boldsymbol\mu_2
\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}
\Sigma_{11} & \Sigma_{12}\\
\Sigma_{21} & \Sigma_{22}
\end{pmatrix}
\right],
$$

the conditional distribution is

$$
\mathbf Y_2\mid \mathbf Y_1
\sim
N(\boldsymbol\mu_{2\cdot1},\Sigma_{2\cdot1}),
$$

where

$$
\boldsymbol\mu_{2\cdot1}
=
\boldsymbol\mu_2
+\Sigma_{21}\Sigma_{11}^{-1}
(\mathbf Y_1-\boldsymbol\mu_1)
$$

and

$$
\Sigma_{2\cdot1}
=
\Sigma_{22}
-\Sigma_{21}\Sigma_{11}^{-1}\Sigma_{12}.
$$

# Spatial regression model

Consider the spatial model

$$
Y(\mathbf s)
=
\mathbf x(\mathbf s)^T\boldsymbol\beta
+W(\mathbf s)+\epsilon(\mathbf s),
$$

where

$$
\mathbf W\sim N\{\mathbf 0,\sigma^2H(\phi)\},
\qquad
\boldsymbol\epsilon\sim N(\mathbf 0,\tau^2I_n),
$$

and the spatial effects and measurement errors are independent. Let

$$
\boldsymbol\theta
=
(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2,\phi).
$$

For the observations at locations
$\mathbf s_1,\ldots,\mathbf s_n$,

$$
\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\theta,X
\sim
N_n \left(
X\boldsymbol\beta,
\sigma^2H(\phi)+\tau^2I_n
\right).
$$

We wish to predict

$$
Y_0=Y(\mathbf s_0)
$$

at a new location $\mathbf s_0$ with covariate vector $\mathbf x_0$.

# Joint distribution of $\mathbf y$ and $Y_0$

Define the spatial correlation vector

$$
\mathbf h_0(\phi)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\operatorname{Cor}\{W(\mathbf s_1),W(\mathbf s_0)\}\\
\vdots\\
\operatorname{Cor}\{W(\mathbf s_n),W(\mathbf s_0)\}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For an exponential correlation function,

$$
[\mathbf h_0(\phi)]_i
=
\exp\{-\phi\lVert\mathbf s_i-\mathbf s_0\rVert\}.
$$

Conditional on $\boldsymbol\theta$,

$$
E(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\theta)=X\boldsymbol\beta,
\qquad
E(Y_0\mid\boldsymbol\theta)=\mathbf x_0^T\boldsymbol\beta,
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\sigma^2H(\phi)+\tau^2I_n.
$$

If $Y_0$ represents a new noisy observation, then

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_0\mid\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\sigma^2+\tau^2.
$$

Because measurement errors at distinct locations are independent,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf y,Y_0\mid\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\sigma^2\mathbf h_0(\phi),
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\sigma^2\mathbf h_0(\phi)^T.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf y\\
Y_0
\end{pmatrix}
\bigg|\boldsymbol\theta,X,\mathbf x_0
\sim
N\left[
\begin{pmatrix}
X\boldsymbol\beta\\
\mathbf x_0^T\boldsymbol\beta
\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma^2H(\phi)+\tau^2I_n & \sigma^2\mathbf h_0(\phi)\\
\sigma^2\mathbf h_0(\phi)^T & \sigma^2+\tau^2
\end{pmatrix}
\right].
$$

# Why the order in the covariance matters

For random vectors $A$ and $B$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(A,B)
=
E\left[(A-EA)(B-EB)^T\right].
$$

Consequently,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(B,A)
=
\operatorname{Cov}(A,B)^T.
$$

Here, $Y_0$ is a scalar and $\mathbf y$ is an $n\times1$ column vector. Thus,

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\sigma^2\mathbf h_0(\phi)^T
}
$$

is a $1\times n$ row vector, whereas

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf y,Y_0\mid\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\sigma^2\mathbf h_0(\phi)
}
$$

is an $n\times1$ column vector. They contain the same covariance values, but one is the transpose of the other.

This orientation is required in the conditional-normal formula. Taking
$\mathbf Y_1=\mathbf y$ and $Y_2=Y_0$ gives

$$
\Sigma_{21}
=
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\theta)
$$

and

$$
\Sigma_{12}
=
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf y,Y_0\mid\boldsymbol\theta).
$$

The dimensions in the conditional mean are

$$
\underbrace{\Sigma_{21}}_{1\times n}
\underbrace{\Sigma_{11}^{-1}}_{n\times n}
\underbrace{(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu_1)}_{n\times1},
$$

which produce a scalar. Similarly,

$$
\underbrace{\Sigma_{21}}_{1\times n}
\underbrace{\Sigma_{11}^{-1}}_{n\times n}
\underbrace{\Sigma_{12}}_{n\times1}
$$

is a scalar, as required for the conditional variance of $Y_0$.

# Stage 1: Conditional prediction for fixed $\boldsymbol\theta$

Match the spatial model to the partitioned-normal notation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf Y_1&=\mathbf y,
&Y_2&=Y_0,\\
\boldsymbol\mu_1&=X\boldsymbol\beta,
&\mu_2&=\mathbf x_0^T\boldsymbol\beta,\\
\Sigma_{11}&=\sigma^2H(\phi)+\tau^2I_n,
&\Sigma_{22}&=\sigma^2+\tau^2,\\
\Sigma_{12}&=\sigma^2\mathbf h_0(\phi),
&\Sigma_{21}&=\sigma^2\mathbf h_0(\phi)^T.
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the conditional-normal formula gives

$$
Y_0\mid\mathbf y,\boldsymbol\theta,\mathbf x_0
\sim
N\{m_0(\boldsymbol\theta),v_0(\boldsymbol\theta)\},
$$

where

$$
\boxed{
m_0(\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\mathbf x_0^T\boldsymbol\beta
+\sigma^2\mathbf h_0(\phi)^T
\{\sigma^2H(\phi)+\tau^2I_n\}^{-1}
(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta)
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
v_0(\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\sigma^2+\tau^2
-\sigma^4\mathbf h_0(\phi)^T
\{\sigma^2H(\phi)+\tau^2I_n\}^{-1}
\mathbf h_0(\phi)
}.
$$

The term $\sigma^4$ arises because

$$
(\sigma^2\mathbf h_0^T)
\Sigma_{11}^{-1}
(\sigma^2\mathbf h_0)
=
\sigma^4\mathbf h_0^T\Sigma_{11}^{-1}\mathbf h_0.
$$

# Stage 2: Integrate over posterior uncertainty in $\boldsymbol\theta$

The distribution derived above treats $\boldsymbol\theta$ as fixed. The posterior predictive distribution in equation (6.19) must also incorporate uncertainty about $\boldsymbol\theta$. By the law of total probability,

$$
p(y_0\mid\mathbf y,X,\mathbf x_0)
=
\int
p(y_0\mid\mathbf y,\boldsymbol\theta,\mathbf x_0)
p(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathbf y,X)
\,d\boldsymbol\theta.
$$

Suppose MCMC provides $G$ draws

$$
\boldsymbol\theta^{(1)},\ldots,\boldsymbol\theta^{(G)}
\sim
p(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathbf y,X).
$$

Monte Carlo integration approximates the posterior integral by

$$
\boxed{
p(y_0\mid\mathbf y,X,\mathbf x_0)
\approx
\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}
p(y_0\mid\mathbf y,\boldsymbol\theta^{(g)},\mathbf x_0)
}
$$

which is equation (6.19).

For draw $g$, define

$$
\boldsymbol\theta^{(g)}
=
\left(
\boldsymbol\beta^{(g)},
\sigma^{2(g)},
\tau^{2(g)},
\phi^{(g)}
\right).
$$

Then

$$
p(y_0\mid\mathbf y,\boldsymbol\theta^{(g)},\mathbf x_0)
=
N\{y_0;m_0^{(g)},v_0^{(g)}\},
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_0^{(g)}
={}&
\mathbf x_0^T\boldsymbol\beta^{(g)}\\
&+\sigma^{2(g)}\mathbf h_0\{\phi^{(g)}\}^T
\left[
\sigma^{2(g)}H\{\phi^{(g)}\}
+\tau^{2(g)}I_n
\right]^{-1}
(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta^{(g)})
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
v_0^{(g)}
={}&
\sigma^{2(g)}+\tau^{2(g)}\\
&-\{\sigma^{2(g)}\}^2
\mathbf h_0\{\phi^{(g)}\}^T
\left[
\sigma^{2(g)}H\{\phi^{(g)}\}
+\tau^{2(g)}I_n
\right]^{-1}
\mathbf h_0\{\phi^{(g)}\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, equation (6.19) can be written as

$$
\boxed{
p(y_0\mid\mathbf y,X,\mathbf x_0)
\approx
\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}
N\{y_0;m_0^{(g)},v_0^{(g)}\}
}.
$$

# Interpretation

Equation (6.19) is generally a **mixture of normal distributions**, rather than one normal distribution:

1. For each posterior draw $\boldsymbol\theta^{(g)}$, the conditional-normal formula supplies one normal predictive distribution.
2. Averaging these $G$ normal densities accounts for posterior uncertainty in the model parameters.
3. The within-component variance $v_0^{(g)}$ represents predictive uncertainty conditional on $\boldsymbol\theta^{(g)}$.
4. Variation in $m_0^{(g)}$ and $v_0^{(g)}$ across draws represents parameter uncertainty.

Thus, the conditional-normal calculation supplies each term on the right-hand side of equation (6.19), while Monte Carlo averaging over the posterior draws produces the complete posterior predictive distribution.

# Note on predicting the latent spatial surface

The result above predicts a new noisy observation $Y_0$, so its marginal variance contains $\sigma^2+\tau^2$. If the target is instead the latent mean

$$
\eta_0=\mathbf x_0^T\boldsymbol\beta+W(\mathbf s_0),
$$

then replace $\Sigma_{22}=\sigma^2+\tau^2$ by $\Sigma_{22}=\sigma^2$. The conditional mean remains unchanged, but the conditional variance becomes

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\eta_0\mid\mathbf y,\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\sigma^2
-\sigma^4\mathbf h_0(\phi)^T
\{\sigma^2H(\phi)+\tau^2I_n\}^{-1}
\mathbf h_0(\phi).
$$
